# Belt, rope and chain drives (`belt_drive`)

<!-- generated by scripts/build_techtree.py from techtree/core/manufacturing.yaml — do not edit -->

- Category: Tools, machines & manufacturing (`manufacturing`)
- Deps: helped by spinning_wheel, textile_fibres
- Core idea: An endless band round two wheels carries rotation from one shaft to another some distance away. The speeds are in inverse proportion to the diameters, so a large wheel driving a small pulley gives high speed (a spinning wheel's spindle, a lathe); crossing the band reverses the direction. A flat leather belt stays on a pulley whose rim is slightly higher in the middle (crowned), because a belt climbs towards the larger diameter. A belt slips under overload, which protects the machine. A chain on toothed wheels cannot slip and keeps exact timing. In a factory one water wheel or engine turns a long overhead shaft from which each machine takes its drive by a belt, with a loose pulley beside the fast one for stopping.
- Pitfalls:
  - Flat or hollow pulley rims: the belt runs off. The rim must be crowned
  - A belt too slack or too tight; and damp changes the length of leather and rope
  - Unguarded belts and shafts, a chief cause of factory injuries
- History: china: c. 15 BC – belt-driven quilling wheel for silk mentioned by Yang Xiong; 976 and 1090 chain drive in the astronomical clocks of Zhang Sixun and Su Song; islamic: 1206 – al-Jazari's chain-of-pots machines; belt-driven spinning wheel shown in Baghdad in 1237; europe: c. 1280 – spinning wheel band drive; c. 1430 belt-driven grindstone; 1790s line shafting in cotton mills; 1880 Renold's bush roller chain; americas: 1828 – Paul Moody at Lowell replaces gear shafting by leather belts, afterwards the American standard
- Read:
  - Joseph Needham, Science and Civilisation in China, Vol. 4 Part 2: Mechanical Engineering (1965)
  - Lynn White Jr., Medieval Technology and Social Change (1962)
